cultural.vision_reason: A Burmese parabaik-style manuscript folding book illustrating a Jataka/Nidana-katha scene with a pavilion, courtiers, and Burmese script text, matching traditional Bamar court painting conventions (theatrical architecture, flat perspective) as noted by Lowry.

physical.medium_raw: Gouache on thick paper, with reinforced paper covers, lacquered and gilded (thitsi)
physical.physical_description:
12 folding pages with illustrations and accompanying text of incidents from the Nidana-katha (introduction to the Jataka stories) between a pair of red covers.

In various colours with a leaning towards rich blues, greens and reds. "The style, while evidently owing much to late Indian painting, has markedly national characteristics, which make it unmistakably Burmese. These can be seen in the conventional rendering of a mountain and of architecture, which is treated in a two dimensional way similar to theatrical scenery". John Lowry, "Burmese Art", 1974.
physical.summary:
The volume from which this painting is taken contains illustrations of incidents from the Nidana-katha, which is the introduction to the Jataka stories and may be part of a set of several volumes comprising this introduction.  

These stories of the Buddha in his previous incarnations provide examples of moral conduct and socially approved responses to situations. They are thus an unlimited source of themes for literature, art and the theatre. The Nidana-katha and the Jataka stories are popular subjects for Burmese illustrated books, many of which have found their way into European collections. The style, while owing much to late Indian painting, has unmistakable Burmese characteristics, such as the conventional rendering of a mountain and of architecture, which is treated two-dimensionally, in a way suggestive of theatrical scenery.

physical.physical_description:
All the boxes are patterned in light red, green and yellow on a green on black hatch-stroke ground with their interiors finished in red lacquer
The common pattern of the six boxes is the gwin-shet (linked cellular design).
The common theme is the signs of the zodiac and days of the week.
The rim of each box and cover is encircled with a narrow border of repeating lotus flowers.
The central motif on the base of each box is set within a circular band of fine lines.

physical.physical_description:
Folding manuscript (Burmese. parabaik). The pages are uncoloured and the text is written in black Burmese round  script. The borders of the pages are illuminated. The cover of the manuscript is lacquered and gilded relief moulded  (Burmese. thayo) card with glass inlay (Burmese. hman-zi shwei-cha) and foliate decorative motifs.

The title on the front cover translates to "Song in glorification of the Holy and High Buddha." The manuscript is  understood to be a volume of verses (Burmese. ei-gyin) extolling the glorious achievements of past ancestors of the Konbaung Dynastyy as well as cradle songs, music and eulogies to be recited and sung to the eldest daughter of King Thibaw and Queen Supayalat on the occasion of piercing her ears 10th day after in the Burmese year 1243 (1882).

deep.objectHistory:
This folding manuscript was presented by Mingyi Mindin Maha Sithu, a prominent Grand Minister and Wundauk (or Vice-Minister) of the  Konbaung Dynasty (1752–1885), to the eldest daughter of King Thibaw Min (r. 1878–1885) and Queen Supayalat (r. 1878–1885). It was  given in celebration of an important ceremony held on the occasion when the child was placed in an emerald cradle on the 10th day after  the new moon of the month of Nadaw in the Burmese year 1243 (December 1882 CE) at the Mandalay Palace, Myanmar.

According to museum records, this manuscript was taken from the private apartments of Queen Supayalat at Mandalay Palace after it was  captured by the British during the Third Anglo-Burmese War in 1885

Given by Colonel Horace Barnet, 9 Lincoln Hoise, Basil Street, London, S.W.3. This acquisition information reflects that found in the  Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

See V&A Registered Paper 1918-3770M

cultural.vision_reason: This is a lacquered teak scripture box with a decorative shrine (used for storing Buddhist manuscripts) made in Burma with typical Bamar motifs (nats, biluus, hti finial) — a genuine Bamar craft object, though it's a container/architectural object rather than a painting or manuscript itself.

physical.medium_raw: Teak, encrusted with coloured glass and stones embedded in gilt thitsi lacquer composition
physical.physical_description: A box surmounted by a small shrine. The colours are dull green and lead colour, relieved here and there with a sober red. The front of the box has a border of repeat tonaya (composite animal) and lotus heads. Central scene shows two pairs of fighting Bilus and two holding lotus stems. In the back there is a cupboard door for access to the manuscripts. The surmounting shrine has three roofs and a hti (finial). In front is a open porch flanked by two openwork panels with nat yok (reverential spirit figures). Teak, encrusted with coloured glass and stones embedded in gilt thitsi lacquer composition using the thayo (relief moulded lacquer) hman-zi shwei-cha (glass inlay) technique
physical.summary: A Buddha image would have been placed within the open porch of this late 19th century teak hpaya khan (Buddhist shrine) which came from a monastery situated near Mandalay. Such sumptuous pieces were often commissioned as acts of merit by royalty or wealthy personages and given to the monkhood. Unusually this hpaya khan rests on its own sadaik (manuscript box) which has a door at the back for access to the manuscripts. The virtuoso carving of Burmese foliate designs and mythical creatures seen on this hpaya khan has been embellished with thayo, or moulded lacquer, encrusted with glass inlay work. A technique which grew in popularity in Burma from the middle of the 18th century and is thought to have been introduced from Thailand.
